semantics.note: Revision 2 keeps 'most likely to benefit' and 'the idea, not necessarily the reality'. It is framed as an observation, but it is really an interpretive judgment about incentives and gives no measure.

contract.note: The contract fairly treats this as commentary that cannot be scored. Testing it as a count of who holds financial stakes would test a narrower claim than the one he made.

reviews.rationale: This is a comparative judgment about who stands to gain from a belief. There is no agreed measure of who is 'most likely to benefit', so no evidence could confirm or refute it. The packet has no evidence items, and that is appropriate here.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words, in a sidenote about benchmarks.

semantics.note: Faithful to his present-tense description. The contract rightly leaves the general maxim unscored and notes that he made no accusation of actual cheating.

contract.note: The plain reading is ordinary: results rest on trust, and no binding enforcement or independent check exists. The target period (from SimpleQA's release to the post date) fits his present tense.

evidence.note: This is the benchmark publisher's own documentation. SimpleQA was open-sourced, answers included, and vendors run it on their own models. It describes no safeguard against tuning on the answers.
From Jan 2025, within the period. The only safeguard against OpenAI training on FrontierMath was a verbal agreement. A holdout set existed, but it is not an enforcement mechanism.
Epoch's lead mathematician said OpenAI's score had not been independently verified and that Epoch relied on trust for now.
The April 2025 LMArena response to the Llama 4 episode came after the target period. It shows a policy update, not a penalty. Context only.

reviews.rationale: Evidence from inside the target period shows vendors scoring themselves on public tests (SimpleQA) and a frontier math benchmark protected only by a verbal agreement, with scores not independently verified. Nothing in the packet shows binding audits, enforceable rules, or penalties in the period. The holdout set is a partial check, but it had not yet been used.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words, presented as his own analysis.

semantics.note: The normalised wording keeps 'does not appear' and the conditions about debt or stake sales. But the statement is explicitly hedged ('based on my analysis', 'does not appear'), which signals lowered confidence.

contract.note: The contract admits the wording is hedged and applies a plain reading anyway. Policy limits plain readings to firm language. It also replaces a claim about SoftBank's ability with a test of how SoftBank actually paid, which is the evaluator's choice, not the speaker's.

evidence.note: Reports SoftBank's Nov 2025 disclosure: it sold its Nvidia shares and part of T-Mobile and took an Arm margin loan for OpenAI. This fits the plain reading, but the claim is hedged and not scored.
Dow Jones report of SoftBank's Feb 2026 disclosure: $27B of new debt plus stake sales helped fund the $22.5B OpenAI payment. Consistent with the plain reading, but not scored.
The CFO's comment on loan-to-value speaks to how risky the debt was, not to whether new funding was needed.

reviews.rationale: 'Based on my analysis, does not appear to have the money' is a hedged judgment, comparable to 'I suspect'. Under the policy, hedged language is not scored, and a plain reading cannot be applied to it. The evidence is consistent with his view: SoftBank did borrow heavily and sell stakes. But the claim stays unscored.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words, in his summary of the CoreWeave, OpenAI and SoftBank chain of dependencies.

semantics.note: A firm present-tense claim about both companies. The 'even if' clause is rhetorical framing, and the clause about prospects is opinion.

contract.note: Reading 'lose' as annual net loss in the latest full year (2024) is the ordinary reading. A cash-burn reading is possible from his '$15B burn' line nearby, but that line is about 2025. The contract makes this explicit and rules contradiction if either company lost under $1B.

evidence.note: From CoreWeave's S-1: a 2024 net loss of about $863M, under $1B, with positive operating income.
CNBC confirmed OpenAI expected about a $5B loss in 2024, based on company documents. It is an expectation from Sept 2024, not an audited figure, but it is enough for 'billions'.

reviews.rationale: The claim says both companies lose billions a year. OpenAI's roughly $5B 2024 loss fits that part. CoreWeave's 2024 net loss was about $863M, below the contract's $1B line. Because the claim covers both companies, the CoreWeave figure meets the contradiction condition. The OpenAI part holds.
